What Are Physical Properties?

Every material has a set of physical properties — measurable characteristics that describe how it behaves under real-world conditions. When an engineer selects a material for a product, they match the properties of available materials to the demands the product will face. Get the match wrong and the product fails; get it right and the product works reliably throughout its designed lifetime.

The specification lists ten physical properties you must be able to describe, distinguish and apply. This lesson covers all ten, then shows how they combine when selecting materials for four specific products: mobile phones, home security alarms, bicycles and children’s play area equipment.

Key Fact

The ten physical properties are: tensile strength, compressive strength, hardness, toughness, malleability, ductility, conductivity, corrosion resistance, environmental degradation and elasticity. Examiners expect you to describe each one precisely — they are not synonyms.

Strength: Tensile and Compressive

Tensile strength is a material’s ability to resist a pulling (tensile) force without breaking. A steel cable supporting a suspension bridge must have high tensile strength — the force in the cable is always a pull. Steel and most metals have high tensile strength; ceramics and cast iron have relatively low tensile strength because they are brittle.

Compressive strength is a material’s ability to resist a squeezing (compressive) force without deforming or cracking. Concrete has high compressive strength, which is why it is used for columns and foundations. In contrast, concrete has low tensile strength — steel reinforcing bars are embedded to compensate for this weakness.

Hardness is a material’s resistance to surface indentation or scratching. A hard material like tool steel resists the cutting forces of a drill bit; a glass screen is hard enough to resist scratching by keys. However, hardness and toughness are different properties — a hard material is not necessarily tough.

Toughness is a material’s ability to absorb energy and resist fracture under impact. Glass is hard but not tough — it resists scratching but shatters under impact. Mild steel is both hard enough and tough: it can absorb an impact without cracking. A bicycle frame material must be tough so that a sudden bump or collision does not cause the frame to fracture suddenly.

Exam tip on this distinction: if a question asks why a product needs toughness rather than just hardness, your answer must mention impact energy absorption and resistance to fracture — not just resistance to scratching.

Malleability and Ductility

Malleability is the ability of a material to be shaped by compressive forces — rolled into sheets, hammered into shapes, or pressed into moulds — without cracking. Copper and aluminium are both malleable, making them suitable for pressing into complex shapes such as car body panels or electrical connectors.

Ductility is the ability of a material to be stretched into a wire or rod without breaking. Copper is highly ductile: it can be drawn into the thin wires used inside electrical cables. A material can be malleable without being ductile, and vice versa, so the exam expects you to use the correct term for the correct process.

Conductivity: Electrical and Thermal

Electrical conductivity is the ease with which a material allows an electric current to flow through it. Copper is an excellent electrical conductor — it is the most widely used material for wiring. Plastics are electrical insulators: they have very low conductivity and are used to coat cables and encase electrical components to prevent electric shock.

Thermal conductivity is the ease with which a material allows heat to flow through it. Metals generally conduct heat well; plastics and ceramics are poor thermal conductors. These two conductivities often move in the same direction (metals conduct both electricity and heat), but this is not always the case, so treat them as separate properties.

Key Fact

Copper is used for electrical wiring because it has very high electrical conductivity — it allows current to flow with very low resistance. Its ductility means it can be drawn into thin wire. Both properties must be stated when justifying copper as a wiring material.

Corrosion Resistance and Environmental Degradation

Corrosion resistance is a material’s ability to resist chemical attack by substances in its environment, most commonly water, oxygen, acids or salts. Stainless steel is chosen for outdoor structures partly because its chromium content creates a protective oxide layer that resists corrosion. Mild steel, by contrast, corrodes readily in damp air unless it is painted, plated or coated.

Environmental degradation is the broader process by which materials deteriorate due to environmental exposure over time. UV light breaks down many plastics, causing them to become brittle and discolour. Temperature cycling can fatigue metals. Engineers working on outdoor products — such as play area equipment — must account for all the environmental factors the product will face over its working life.

Elasticity

Elasticity is the ability of a material to return to its original shape after a deforming force is removed. A spring steel returns to its shape after being compressed or stretched. Rubber is also highly elastic. When a material is stretched beyond its elastic limit, it deforms permanently — this is called plastic deformation. Engineers must ensure that materials in springs and flexible components operate within their elastic limit in normal service.

Mobile phone casing and screen: The casing must be hard (to resist scratches from keys and coins), tough (to survive drops), and have low electrical conductivity (to be safe to handle). The screen must also be hard and have good optical clarity; some glass formulations are engineered to be tougher than standard glass.

Home security alarm housing and sensor: The outer casing must have good corrosion resistance and resist environmental degradation (UV, damp) because it may be mounted outside. Electrical components inside require materials with high electrical conductivity for wiring and low electrical conductivity for the casing — to prevent short circuits. The casing must be tough enough to resist deliberate tampering.

Bicycle frame: The frame must have high tensile strength (pedalling and rider weight create pulling forces in the frame tubes), good toughness (to survive kerb drops and collisions without fracturing), and low density so that the bike remains light. Aluminium alloy frames balance these requirements: aluminium is not as strong as steel, but it is much lighter, so larger-diameter tubes are used to compensate. Good corrosion resistance is also important for a product used outdoors in wet conditions.

Children’s play area equipment: Safety is the primary concern. Materials must have high toughness (impact from children climbing and falling), good corrosion resistance (outdoor environment, rain), resistance to environmental degradation (UV light degrades plastics over time), and smooth surfaces to prevent injuries. Rubber impact surfaces beneath equipment also rely on high elasticity to absorb landing impacts safely.

What Is an Engineering Drawing?

A written description of a component leaves too much to interpretation. An engineering drawing communicates shape, size, and detail in a form that any trained engineer anywhere can read without ambiguity. The conventions used in engineering drawings are standardised in Britain under BS 8888 — the British Standard for technical product documentation. Knowing these conventions is not just useful background; the exam tests your ability to interpret and produce drawings to these standards.

Third-Angle Orthographic Projection

Third-angle orthographic projection is the system this course requires you to use. British Standard BS 8888 permits both first-angle and third-angle projection, so a drawing must always carry the symbol that says which one it uses. It shows an object as three flat views — front, plan (top) and end (side) — laid out on paper according to a fixed rule: the view of the top sits above the front view, and the view of the right-hand side sits to the right of the front view. Think of the object being placed inside a transparent glass box; the views are projected onto the glass walls nearest to each face, then the walls are unfolded flat.

Third-angle projection uses a specific symbol: a truncated cone drawn in side view, with the smaller circular end of the cone on the right. You will often see this symbol in the title block of a drawing. Always check for it when reading a drawing — if it is absent or shows first-angle projection (where the views are arranged on the opposite sides), the layout will be different and you risk misreading dimensions.

Key Fact

In third-angle projection (the system this course uses): the top view (plan) sits above the front view, and the right-side view sits to the right of the front view. The symbol is a truncated cone with the small circle on the right. Do not confuse this with first-angle projection, which places views on the opposite sides.

The Three Views in Orthographic Projection

A typical orthographic drawing uses three standard views:

Front view (elevation): The most informative face of the object. It is usually chosen to show the greatest number of features clearly. This view is drawn first and the others are projected from it.

Plan view (top view): What the object looks like from directly above. In third-angle projection this view is positioned above the front view.

End view (side view): What the object looks like from one side. In third-angle projection the right-side view is placed to the right of the front view.

All three views share the same scale and are drawn in alignment — features that appear in one view project directly across to the same position in the adjacent view. This alignment allows you to locate any feature precisely in three dimensions from a flat drawing.

Standard Line Types (BS 8888)

Different lines carry different meanings in engineering drawings. Using the wrong line type is read by an examiner as a misunderstanding of the drawing convention — so accuracy here matters.

Continuous thick line — Visible edges and outlines of the object as seen from the viewing direction. These are the most prominent lines on the drawing.

Continuous thin line — Dimension lines, leader lines, projection lines and hatching lines. Thin because they should not compete visually with the outline.

Thin dashed line — Hidden detail: edges or features that exist on the object but are not visible from the current viewing direction (for example, a drilled hole seen from above, or an internal pocket seen from the front).

Thin chain line (long-dash short-dash) — Centre lines: the axes of holes, cylinders, arcs and lines of symmetry. These run through the centre of any circular or symmetrical feature.

Thick chain line — Cutting plane: shows where an imaginary cut has been made through the object to create a sectional view.

Key Fact

Five BS 8888 line types: continuous thick (visible edges), continuous thin (dimensions/leaders), thin dashed (hidden edges), thin chain (centre lines), thick chain (cutting plane). Each carries a specific meaning — using the wrong line for a feature is an error.

Scenario: A front view of a metal bracket shows a rectangular outline, a dashed rectangular shape inside the outline, thin lines with arrows and numbers running between the outline and the edge, and a long-dash short-dash line running vertically through the centre.

Interpreting the lines:
• The rectangular outline — continuous thick line: the visible edges of the bracket as seen from the front.
• The dashed rectangle inside — thin dashed line: a rectangular slot or recess cut into the back face of the bracket, not visible from the front (hidden detail).
• The thin lines with numbers — continuous thin dimension lines with arrowheads showing the width and height of the bracket in mm.
• The long-dash short-dash line — thin chain centre line: the bracket is symmetrical about this vertical axis.

Being able to identify these four distinct line types from a description is the kind of task the exam may set. Practise naming the line type and explaining its meaning in one sentence each.

Isometric Projection — A 3D Picture

Isometric projection is used alongside orthographic views to give a clear three-dimensional impression of an object. Three axes are used: one vertical and two running at 30° either side of the horizontal. Lengths are drawn true to scale along these three axes only — diagonal and curved features must be constructed indirectly (by plotting points along the axes and connecting them). Circles in isometric projection become ellipses.

Isometric projection is not a view from a specific angle in the way orthographic projection is. It is a convention that produces consistent, proportionally correct pictures. It is particularly useful for assembly drawings and instructions because the shape of the part is immediately clear to anyone, including non-specialists.

Sectional Views — Cutting to See Inside

Some internal features — such as bores, internal threads, or recesses — are difficult to describe with dashed lines alone. A sectional view imagines the object sliced along a flat plane. The cut is shown in the other views using the thick chain cutting plane line, with arrows indicating the direction of view. The cut surfaces exposed by the imaginary saw cut are shown with hatching — evenly spaced diagonal lines drawn at 45°. Thin, consistent hatching lines distinguish material from empty space and are drawn across the entire cut face.

The section label is typically written as “Section A–A” (or B–B, C–C for multiple sections on the same drawing). The letters appear at each end of the cutting plane line to identify which section view corresponds to which cut.

Scenario: A drawing of a cylindrical housing shows a front orthographic view and a side view. On the front view, a thick chain line (cutting plane) runs horizontally across the centre, labelled “A–A” with arrows pointing downward. A separate view labelled “Section A–A” shows the inside of the housing with hatching at 45° covering the top and bottom walls, and a clear circular bore in the centre with no hatching (empty space).

Reading the section: The hatched areas represent the solid metal walls of the housing that have been cut through. The un-hatched circle in the middle is the hollow bore — empty space through which a shaft or pipe would pass. Without the sectional view, this internal bore would only be visible as a dashed circle in the front view, which is less clear.

When drawing or interpreting sectional views, remember: hatching covers only the material that the cutting plane has physically sliced through. Features beyond the cut plane (visible in the background) are drawn as normal outlines, not hatched.

Datums and Dimensions on Drawings

Just as dimensions in a workshop are measured from a datum point or line, engineering drawings record dimensions from a datum. A drawing datum prevents cumulative measurement error in the workshop. All dimensions are written in millimetres by default on UK engineering drawings unless another unit is stated. Dimension lines are continuous thin lines with arrowheads touching the projection lines that frame the feature being dimensioned. The number sits above or in a gap in the dimension line.

Why Safe Working Matters

Engineering workshops contain real risks: rotating machinery, sharp tools, hot flames, electrical equipment and heavy materials. Every year people are seriously injured in workshops through unsafe practice. Safe working is not an add-on to engineering — it is a fundamental part of the engineer’s job. In a professional engineering company, failure to follow safe working procedures can result in criminal prosecution under health and safety law. In a school or college workshop, the same principles apply.

The legal framework for workplace health and safety in Great Britain begins with the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. This Act places a duty on employers to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health, safety and welfare of their employees. It also places duties on employees to take reasonable care of themselves and others, and to cooperate with their employer’s safety arrangements. Two important sets of regulations made under this Act are the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998 (PUWER) and the Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992.

Key Fact

A risk assessment is a systematic process with three stages: (1) identify the hazards; (2) assess the risk (likelihood and severity of harm); (3) decide and implement control measures. You must be able to distinguish between a hazard and a risk — they are not the same thing.

Hazard and Risk: The Critical Distinction

A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm. A spinning lathe chuck is a hazard. A bottle of solvent is a hazard. A trailing power cable on the workshop floor is a hazard. The hazard exists regardless of whether anyone is actually harmed.

Risk is the combination of two factors: how likely is it that the hazard will actually cause harm, and how severe would that harm be? A spinning lathe chuck has a high severity (the injury would be serious) but a lower likelihood if the operator is trained and the guard is in place. A risk assessment evaluates both factors together. A risk that is highly likely and would cause severe injury requires urgent control measures; a risk that is unlikely and would cause only minor harm may be managed with a simple safety rule.

Task: Drill a 10 mm hole in a piece of mild steel using a pillar drill.

Step 1 — Identify hazards:
• Rotating drill bit (contact causes lacerations or amputation).
• Workpiece snagging and spinning (impact injury to hands and body).
• Metal swarf/cuttings ejected from the hole (eye injury).
• Loose clothing or hair drawn into the spindle (entanglement, severe injury).
• Noise from machine operation (hearing damage with prolonged exposure).

Step 2 — Assess risk (likelihood × severity for each):
Workpiece spinning: HIGH severity (broken bones, lacerations), HIGH likelihood if not clamped → HIGH risk. Must be controlled before work begins.
Eye injury from swarf: MEDIUM severity (could cause permanent eye damage), MEDIUM likelihood without eye protection → MEDIUM-HIGH risk.

Step 3 — Control measures:
• Clamp the workpiece in a machine vice secured to the drill table — reduces the risk of the workpiece spinning if the drill bit snags.
• Wear safety goggles — reduces the risk of eye injury from swarf.
• Tie back long hair; tuck in loose clothing and remove jewellery — reduces the risk of entanglement.
• Ensure the drill guard is in position before switching on — reduces contact risk with the rotating bit.
• Remove the chuck key before switching the machine on — eliminates chuck-key ejection hazard.

The Hierarchy of Control Measures

Control measures are ranked in a hierarchy of control from most effective to least effective. The hierarchy must be applied in order: always seek the highest-level control measure possible before resorting to a lower one.

  • Elimination — remove the hazard entirely. If a task can be redesigned so that the hazard does not exist, this is always the best option. For example, if a chemical solvent is not needed for a task, not using it eliminates the hazard.
  • Substitution — replace the hazard with something less dangerous. Replace a highly toxic solvent with a less hazardous cleaning agent. Replace a sharp metal burr with a plastic edge protector.
  • Engineering controls — use physical barriers or design changes to separate people from the hazard. Machine guards, interlocks (the machine cannot start with the guard open), extraction systems for fumes and dust, and Local Exhaust Ventilation (LEV) are all engineering controls. They are built into the machine or the workplace — they do not depend on the operator remembering to do something.
  • Administrative controls — use rules, training, signage and working procedures to reduce the likelihood of harm. Safe operating procedures, induction training, warning signs and permit-to-work systems are administrative controls. They rely on people following rules, which makes them less reliable than engineering controls.
  • Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) — provide protective equipment such as safety goggles, gloves, ear defenders, safety footwear and overalls. PPE is the last line of defence — it protects only the individual wearing it and does nothing to reduce the hazard itself. It should be used in conjunction with higher-level controls, not as a substitute for them.
Key Fact

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is always the last resort in the control hierarchy, not the first. Examiners expect you to recognise that putting on goggles is less effective than fitting a machine guard. A top-band answer will state the hierarchy principle, not just list PPE items.

Common PPE in a Workshop

Different tasks require different PPE. Choosing the correct PPE for the task is a skill in itself. Safety goggles protect eyes from swarf, chips and chemical splashes; face shields provide greater coverage for grinding operations. Ear defenders reduce the risk of hearing damage in noisy workshops. Gloves protect hands from cuts and chemical exposure, but must not be worn when using a lathe or drill — they can snag on the rotating parts and pull the hand in. Heat-resistant gloves are needed when brazing or welding. Safety footwear (steel toe-capped boots) protects against dropped materials. Overalls or workshop coats keep loose clothing away from machinery.

Lathe: Never use a file on a rotating lathe workpiece by holding the file in both hands across the rotating part — this risks the file snagging and pulling your arm into the lathe. Remove all swarf with a brush, not by hand. Ensure the chuck guard is in place. Never wear gloves when operating a lathe.

Pillar drill: Always clamp the workpiece — never hold it by hand. Remove the chuck key before switching on. Lower the guard before starting. Wear goggles. Keep hands clear of the spindle during operation.

Brazing hearth: Work in a well-ventilated area or use LEV (extraction) to remove brazing fumes, which can be harmful if inhaled. Wear appropriate eye protection (tinted goggles or a face shield). Use heat-resistant gloves when handling hot workpieces. Allow workpieces to cool fully before handling with bare hands — hot metal looks the same as cold metal.

Bandsaw: Keep fingers well clear of the blade. Use a push stick for narrow pieces. Do not attempt to back out of a cut while the blade is running. Ensure the blade guard is set as close to the workpiece as practicable to minimise the exposed blade length.
